content: Chlamydia trachomatis is a bacterial pathogen that primarily infects the submucosal connective tissue and can spread to regional lymph nodes. Clinically, it often presents as a unilateral, tender swelling of the inguinal or femoral lymph nodes, accompanied by a genital ulcer or papule. In cases of anorectal exposure, symptoms may include proctitis, rectal discharge, pain, constipation, or tenesmus. If left untreated, lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), a condition caused by certain strains of C. trachomatis, can lead to complications such as rectal fistulas or strictures. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued updated guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of C. trachomatis infections. Advances in diagnostic methods over the past decade have significantly improved the detection of this pathogen. While traditional methods such as culture and direct immunofluorescence assays (DFAs) are still used, nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) are now strongly recommended due to their superior sensitivity and specificity. NAATs can be applied to a wide range of sample types, including urine, vulvovaginal, cervical, and urethral swabs. Although NAATs are not yet licensed for extra-genital samples, they have demonstrated reliability in detecting chlamydial infections in rectal and pharyngeal swabs. Additionally, some commercially available tests combine chlamydia and gonorrhea detection, enhancing diagnostic efficiency. The WHO guidelines emphasize the need to update treatment protocols to address changes in the epidemiology and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) patterns of C. trachomatis. LGV, for instance, is increasingly prevalent among men who have sex with men (MSM) in certain regions, and treatment failures with tetracyclines and macrolides have been reported in approximately 10% of cases. The guidelines also highlight the importance of evidence-based recommendations for firstand second-line treatments, ensuring they are informed by the latest clinical data. The primary objectives of these guidelines are to provide evidence-based recommendations for the treatment of C. trachomatis infections, including uncomplicated genital infections, anorectal infections, infections in pregnant women, LGV, and neonatal ophthalmia. The target audience includes healthcare providers at all levels, policymakers, program managers, and professionals involved in sexual and reproductive health programs, particularly in low-, middle-, and high-income countries. The guidelines were developed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology, which assesses the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations. Recommendations are categorized as either strong (e.g., The WHO STI guideline recommends...) or conditional (e.g., The WHO STI guideline suggests...). The decision-making process considered factors such as the balance of benefits and harms, patient values and preferences, resource use, acceptability, equity, and feasibility. To ensure transparency and minimize conflicts of interest, all guideline development group (GDG) members disclosed their interests, which were reviewed and deemed non-significant. The recommendations were finalized through consensus, with no need for voting, and were subsequently peer-reviewed and approved by an external review group. The dissemination of these guidelines will involve printed publications, online resources, and integration into WHO's reproductive health library. Efforts will be made to support countries in adapting and implementing the guidelines, taking into account local AMR patterns, healthcare capacity, and resources. Monitoring and updating the guidelines will be an ongoing process, informed by new evidence and user feedback. In adapting the guidelines for national use, recommended treatments should achieve at least 95% efficacy. Countries are encouraged to conduct high-quality studies to gather local epidemiological data and ensure the guidelines are tailored to their specific STI landscape. Where local data are unavailable, the global recommendations can be adopted as presented. Budgeting for medicines and ensuring their availability are critical to the successful implementation of these guidelines, as access to effective treatment is essential for controlling the spread of infection and preventing complications.
